new_statements.quote: Like most Chadic languages, Mubi is tonal. I have not carried out a detailed analysis of the tone system, so a more complete study of the tone system has yet to be done. [...] As a working hypothesis, I propose that there are only two tonemes, High (H) and Low (L). While I also transcribed Mid (M) tone for some words, there were no examples of Mid tone contrasting with Low tone. Lexically, a handful of examples show contrast between High and Low tone. But I found no evidence that tone is lexically contrastive for verbs (section 3.6). Several different grammatical categories for nouns and verbs are only differentiated by tone. [...] Other than the singular imperative, all verb forms have only low tone.
new_statements.citation: Prickett, Davis. 2012. The phonology and morphology of verb forms in Mubi. MA thesis, University of North Dakota (advisor James S. Roberts). 143 pp. https://commons.und.edu/theses/1370
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, section 2.3 'Tone', pp. 29-30 (PDF pp. 44-45); also footnote 9, p. 35
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (143 pp., text layer; title page 'The phonology and morphology of verb forms in Mubi', Davis Prickett, MA thesis, University of North Dakota, December 2012, commons.und.edu/theses/1370). The quoted passage is at the stated locator verbatim: section '2.3 Tone', thesis pp. 29-30 = PDF pp. 44-45, reads 'Like most Chadic languages, Mubi is tonal. I have not carried out a detailed analysis of the tone system, so a more complete study of the tone system has yet to be done. But Table 14 gives examples of several words contrasting in tone.' then, after Table 14 (Phonemic tone: /na/ L 'cook.PFV' vs H 'boule'; /buɡ/ L 'hip' vs H 'kidney'; /toɡo/ LL 'skin'; /ɗuɟi/ LH 'pimple'; /foso/ HH 'hand';…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mubi is described as a tone language with two tonemes (H, L); lexical tone contrasts exist on nouns (e.g. /buɡ/ L 'hip' vs H 'kidney'; foso HH 'hand', samo HL 'broom'), while verbs are uniformly low-toned except for grammatical high tone (sg. imperative, 1SG possessive on nouns, some pronominal suffixes). The source says nothing at all about word stress or accent, so no stress rule can be stated; the only accent claim in the literature is diachronic (Wolff 1988, via Souag 2021: a pre-Mubi accent position conditioning final-vowel deletion).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone analysis is explicitly provisional ('working hypothesis'); Mid tone transcribed for some words but not shown contrastive; Jungraithmayr (1974, 1978) marks high tone on some verb forms which Prickett could not confirm (p. 35, fn. 9).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (perfective verbs, singular nouns) elicited from two speakers from the Mangalmé area living in Mongo, 2012. Chapter 1 states there is no distinct dialectal variation within Mubi (100% lexical similarity between cantons).
new_statements.identity_note: Prickett 2012 describes the Mubi of the Mangalmé cantons (Mubi Zarga, Mubi Goz, Mubi Hadaba), Guéra, Chad, from two speakers resident in Mongo; he reports no dialectal variation within the language (glottocode mubi1246; endonym monjul/minjile). The closely related Mubic varieties Zerenkel and Masmaje are separate languoids and not covered.

sources.locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, section 2.3 'Tone', pp. 29-30 (PDF pp. 44-45); also footnote 9, p. 35
sources.note: Nothing about stress (zero hits for 'stress'). Ch. 2 Phonology, sect. 2.3 'Tone' pp. 29-30: 'Like most Chadic languages, Mubi is tonal'; working hypothesis of two tonemes H and L; lexical H/L contrast in nouns, none found in verbs; grammatical tone (1SG possessive, sg. imperative, pronominal suffixes); all verb forms low-toned except the sg. imperative. Footnote 9 p. 35: 'Tone is not marked on any forms of the verb since every syllable within the basic verb morphology has low tone.'

sources.note: Only diachronic: final-vowel deletion 'potentially related to pre-Mubi stress position, with vowel deletion after accent in final open syllables, as argued for the verbal system by Wolff (1988: 169)' (postprint p. 8). Tone data quoted from Jungraithmayr 2013: in Arabic-loan plurals 'all tones are low except on the vowel that would be stressed in Arabic' (p. 13-14). No synchronic stress statement.
